strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 37 tasks (Adroit + Meta-World) with 3 random seeds, covering multiple strong baselines including DP3, FlowPolicy, and the closely related MP1
The gradient analysis in Section 4.2 (Eqs. 5-7) provides a clear, plausible geometric motivation for why MSE-trained flow models underperform on low-velocity, high-precision manipulation tasks
The proposed OMP shows meaningful gains on the hardest task categories (e.g., +10.6% over MP1 on Meta-World Very Hard tasks), which is where improvements matter most
The ablation study (Table 2) isolates each component, and the training curves in Figure 4 support claims of improved stability and convergence
Related work is thorough and positions the contribution clearly relative to MP1 and DM1
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the 'Directional Alignment' is a standard cosine-similarity loss, and the 'Differential Derivation Equation' (Eq. 11) is simply a finite-difference approximation of a derivative presented under a new name, without any analysis of approximation error or sensitivity to the perturbation constant epsilon

Potential correctness issue in Eq. 11: the MeanFlow Identity (Eq. 4) involves the total derivative d/dt of u(z_t, r, t), which should account for the change of z_t with t along the trajectory, but the finite-difference scheme perturbs only t while holding z_t fixed; this discrepancy is not discussed and could undermine the DDE proposal

The abstract claims improved 'few-shot generalization' and criticizes MP1's fixed temperature hyperparameters in the Dispersive Loss, but the paper presents no dedicated few-shot generalization experiments and never addresses the temperature issue in the method
The paper is simulation-only (Adroit and Meta-World); no real-robot experiments are provided, limiting evidence for the claimed practical value for 'real-time control'
Reproducibility gaps: no code release is mentioned, and key hyperparameters (lambda_cos, lambda_Disp, epsilon in Eq. 11, network architecture) are not specified

Ablation results contain unexplained anomalies: the '-JVP + DDE' variant outperforms full OMP on Adroit Pen (64 vs. 60), and the average improvement over MP1 (3.4%) is within roughly one standard deviation, so the headline claim rests mainly on the harder task subsets

The theoretical motivation (gradient starvation for small-magnitude targets) is asserted rather than empirically verified; e.g., no experiment isolates low-velocity regimes to show cosine loss specifically helps there

Writing quality is below bar for a main-track submission: numerous typos ('twnety-one', 'decoder decoderθ', 'Mean Policy' in Figure 2, inconsistent 'mp1/MP1'), a garbled sentence in Section 4 opening, and Eq. 11 contains an apparent typo in its arguments

Several key baselines and related methods (MP1, DM1, World4RL, TRDRL, CLAP) are arXiv-only 2025 preprints, and it is unclear whether Table 1 numbers are reproduced or copied, which affects comparability

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 3 Adroit tasks, 34 Meta-World tasks (3 seeds each), and 3 real-world manipulation tasks with 20 trials, comparing against a broad set of recent baselines (DP/DP3, Simple DP3, FlowPolicy, MPI1, CP, AdaFlow) at matched NFE settings.

Clear identification and motivation of three candidate failure modes of MeanFlow applied to robotics (spectral attenuation of the averaged-velocity target, direction/magnitude coupling of MSE in low-velocity regimes, and ~2x activation memory from nested JVP differentiation), each supported by a controlled synthetic experiment or memory measurement (Fig. 2, Table 3, Appendix B/C).

Useful memory analysis (Appendix B.3) showing the JVP-based total derivative roughly doubles activation memory, and a practical finite-difference (DDE) variant that cuts GPU memory substantially (e.g., 26.7GB to 19.2GB) with only a ~1.5% average success-rate drop.

Thorough ablations isolating the Dispersive and Directional Alignment loss terms, plus a sensitivity study over action-chunk horizons (Table 5), and generally good reproducibility details (hyperparameters in Table 4, seeds, training budgets, code in supplementary).
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is heuristic and in places technically flawed. Theorem B.1 treats the averaging operator as pure integration (|U(w)| ~ |V(w)|/|w|), ignoring the time-varying 1/t normalization, so the claimed quadratic PSD decay of the average-velocity target is not rigorously established for the actual MeanFlow target. Similarly, the 'gradient starvation' argument (Eq. 8-9) is a 2D polar-coordinate decomposition; in the Cartesian parametrization networks actually use, the Euclidean gradient does not vanish as rho* -> 0, so the transfer of this pathology to high-dimensional deep policies is asserted rather than demonstrated beyond the toy experiment.

Methodological novelty is limited: the Directional Alignment loss is a standard cosine-similarity auxiliary term, and the DDE is a finite-difference approximation of the JVP borrowed from prior work (Wang et al. 2025c). The contribution is largely an empirical combination of these ingredients on top of MeanFlow.

The 'critical pathology' narrative is undermined by the results: MPI1, which the authors argue suffers from exactly these pathologies, still achieves 78.9% average success vs. OMP's 82.3%. The improvement is modest relative to reported standard deviations (~1.7-2.1%), only 3 seeds are used, and no statistical significance testing is provided.

The DDE approximation introduces finite-difference bias, but the perturbation epsilon is never analyzed or ablated; the cited 'sensitivity analysis in Section E' concerns action-chunk lengths, not epsilon, leaving a key hyperparameter of the proposed method unjustified.

Internal inconsistencies and overclaiming: the conclusion cites 'Numerical Instability in Short-Horizon Denoising' as an analyzed pathology, which does not appear in the paper; phrases like 'rigorous analysis' and 'establishing a new standard' exceed what the evidence supports.

Figure 1's speed-success comparison does not control for backbone/representation differences across methods, so the FPS axis conflates architecture choices with the proposed objective; real-world evaluation is limited to three tasks with one robot setup.

strengths: The paper identifies and analyzes three concrete failure modes (spectral bias from the averaging operator, gradient starvation in low-velocity regimes, and memory cost of nested JVP differentiation) when applying MeanFlow to robot policies. The motivating analyses, including the synthetic sum-of-sines experiment (Fig. 2a, Theorem B.1) and the controlled 2D angular-error experiment (Fig. 2b, Eq. 8-9, B.2), are thoughtful and give the empirical design choices a clear rationale.

The evaluation is broad: 6 Adroit tasks plus 34 Meta-World tasks with 3 random seeds, sensitivity analysis over action-chunk lengths, a loss-component ablation, GPU-memory measurements (Table 3), and three real-robot tasks. The proposed OMP outperforms strong one-step baselines (MPI, FlowPolicy) on average (82.3% vs 78.9% for MPI-JVP on simulation) while retaining NFE=1.

The JVP vs. DDE comparison is honest: the authors report that the finite-difference approximation incurs a measurable performance drop (82.3% -> 80.8%) in exchange for substantial memory savings, and they analyze when each variant is preferable (Table 5).
The paper is generally well organized, with preliminary experiments (Appendix C) that directly validate each claimed pathology before introducing the method.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest and components are assembled from prior work. MPI (Sheng et al., 2025) already applies MeanFlow to manipulation; the Directional Alignment loss is a standard cosine-similarity auxiliary objective, and the DDE is a finite-difference approximation explicitly borrowed from prior work (Wang et al., 2025c; Karakida et al., 2023). The contribution is essentially an incremental refinement of MPI, and the paper's framing as a 'theoretical breakthrough' level advance overstates this.

The claimed improvement over the strongest baseline is small relative to the evaluation noise. On Meta-World Easy tasks MPI already achieves 88.2% vs. OMP's 89.7%; the headline gap is 3.4% average with no statistical significance testing. Real-world gains (10-15%) are based on only 20 trials per task across 3 tasks, which does not establish significance.

The evaluation metric ('top-5 average success' over evaluations every 200 epochs) selects the best checkpoints, which can inflate reported numbers; standard final-checkpoint or last-k averages would be more trustworthy. This protocol detail is easy to miss and weakens comparability with prior reports.

The theory is heuristic rather than rigorous. Theorem B.1 assumes wide-sense stationary velocity processes, an assumption poorly matched to piecewise manipulation trajectories; the gradient-starvation analysis concerns a single 2D vector with frozen weights, and no analysis connects these idealized settings quantitatively to the actual policy-learning losses.

Internal inconsistency: the Conclusion cites 'Numerical Instability in Short-Horizon Denoising' as an identified pathology, but this is never analyzed in the paper (the intro lists spectral bias, gradient starvation, and memory complexity). This suggests rushed writing and undermines confidence in the claims.

Several reproducibility details are missing: loss weights (lambda_dis, lambda_DA) in Eq. 13 are never specified, the finite-difference perturbation epsilon is not given, and no guidance is provided on tuning them; code is only 'included in supplementary material' without stated licensing or verification.
Figure 1 reports ~120 FPS for OMP but the control-frequency measurement protocol (what is timed, per what hardware, with which encoder) is not described, making the efficiency claims hard to verify.

The real-world evaluation (3 tasks, single robot setup) is limited, and the claimed robustness on 'Slip Ring' (40-55% success) still leaves substantial headroom; broader real-robot validation would be needed to support the 'new standard for real-time generative robot control' claim.
